doc.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Depression-era Chicago: jobs, marriage, first bands
title: Whether he ever left music; the piano was a family social thing
summary: He insists he never left music and that the piano was bought for family socials, not his own ambition.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: My understanding is that your entry back into music was – and I say back into music . . .
Yeah. This is where you throw me a little bit, because I never got out of the music.

I was always trying to do something in music, if it was playing the piano, which I wasn’t that great a piano player, enough to make a living out of that. So this was a hustle on the side of anything else that you would try to do.

When I say coming back into it, what we’ve established here is that you had a violin early on, or you took violin lessons. But we haven’t come back to any instrument after that, except that your parents bought a piano. That was, in my understanding, you’re coming back to your passion. Now if I’m wrong . . .
If I’m wrong, let me know.
It wasn’t my idea, that I wanted to play a piano, to have it. That was a social thing for the home.
It happened to be in the house, and your mother – there were social things going on. You began to play it, and you began to see it as a possible hustle. My understanding is that you started playing.
That’s right. I just picked it up.
Okay. Now I just want to get to the bass.
Yeah? What happened as far as the bass is concerned, is that – let me back up to the picture of how I got involved in that. Hold it a minute.
